sentences.text: Gojirasaurus is a theropod dinosaur named after the Japanese movie monster Godzilla, combining the monster's name with the Greek word for lizard to mean 'Godzilla lizard'. The name references the dinosaur's relatively large size compared to other Triassic theropods.
This species is distinguished from its relative Coelophysis by having a more robust tibia, a bone in the lower leg that measured 469 millimeters in length in the known specimen.
Gojirasaurus was one of the largest Triassic theropods, reaching 5.5 to 6 meters in length and weighing at least 150 kg, making it likely the largest carnivore of the Triassic period.

Features of the pelvis and ankle suggest the holotype was an immature individual that could have grown larger in maturity, with adult estimates reaching 6.5 meters in length and weighing approximately 150 to 200 kilograms.

Kenneth Carpenter named Gojirasaurus quayi in 1997 based on holotype specimen UCM 47221 found in Quay County, New Mexico. The fossils were found in the Cañón Toro Formation, part of the Dockum Group, in Revuelto Creek, Quay County, New Mexico, USA. The holotype specimen, known as UCM 47221, is a partial skeleton consisting of teeth, four ribs, and four vertebrae. The specific name 'quayi' refers to Quay County, New Mexico, where the holotype specimen was discovered in 1997.
Its classification suggests Gojirasaurus was a bipedal, terrestrial, and actively mobile carnivore.

Carpenter (1997) formally classified Gojirasaurus within the superfamily Coelophysoidea. Gojirasaurus is classified within the infraorder Coelophysoidea and the family Coelophysidae. In 1997, Carpenter classified Gojirasaurus quayi within the family Coelophysidae.

Rauhut (2003) proposed that taller neural spines on mid and posterior dorsal vertebrae distinguish Gojirasaurus from other coelophysoids. Rauhut attempted to diagnose the genus in 2003 based on higher neural spines on dorsal vertebrae compared to other coelophysids.

Gojirasaurus lived during the Late Triassic Period and includes only one known species. Fossils of Gojirasaurus date to approximately 212 million years ago during the early Revueltian stage. Gojirasaurus lived in North America during the Late Triassic, approximately 218 to 211 million years ago. Gojirasaurus lived during the Norian stage of the Late Triassic, approximately 228 to 208 million years ago.
Contemporaries of Gojirasaurus included the pseudosuchian Shuvosaurus and the phytosaurian Rutiodon.

It is debated whether Gojirasaurus belongs among the coelophysids or within Averostriformes, a grade including Dilophosaurus. There is an ongoing debate about how much of the fossil material actually belongs to a single species. A 2007 study by Nesbitt et al. suggested the vertebrae belonged to the rauisuchian Shuvosaurus while the pubis and tibia belonged to a Coelophysid. It is debated whether the remains of Gojirasaurus represent a single animal or a chimera of mixed fossils. The validity of Gojirasaurus as a distinct genus is doubtful due to conflicting fossil assignments. Mortimer proposed in 2012 that the robust tibia might be related to size rather than being a unique evolutionary trait.
